title: Evaluation of the Impact of Design Parameters on the Acoustic Environment Perceived by Primary Students
research_question: To identify the characteristics of physical learning spaces that influence the acoustic environment perceived by primary students, specifically exploring (i) differences in acoustic environment perception based on learning space type (layout and acoustic treatment) and (ii) associations between design parameters and acoustic environment perception.

participants.description: Primary students aged 8-11 years old (mean age 10 years, SD 1), 59.0% female, 38.7% male, 2.3% non-binary. 98.0% native Spanish speakers. From 19 learning spaces across 9 primary schools in Santiago and Concepción, Chile.
participants.recruitment: Parents provided consent via school managers; students without permission were given an alternative activity or removed from class.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 19 existing primary school learning spaces, categorized into four groups: Traditional without acoustic treatment (TLE.NA, n=5), Traditional with acoustic treatment (TLE.AA, n=3), Flexible without acoustic treatment (FLE.NA, n=9), and Flexible with acoustic treatment (FLE.AA, n=2). Spaces were characterized by geometry (height, floor area, volume), acoustic conditioning (% sound-absorbing material, % glass), window material, potential urban noise sources, spatial density (m²/student), number of learning zones, diversity of furniture, and space adaptability.

measures.instrument: Student questionnaire (adapted from previous IEQ and ISO 28802 standards), 4-point scale (very uncomfortable to not uncomfortable)
Student questionnaire (6 items for different noise sources), 3-point scale (always, sometimes, never) for bothered responses, plus yes/no for hearing the source
Student questionnaire (4 items for hearing teacher/classmates in silent/group tasks), 5-point scale (very well to very bad)
Student questionnaire (1 item: 'How would you prefer the sound environment to be NOW?'), 4-point scale (much quieter to no change)
Acoustic measurements (Ln, dBA) for 15 minutes during occupied conditions
Space checklist (geometry, acoustic conditioning, window material, urban noise sources)
Space checklist (spatial density, learning zones, furniture diversity, space adaptability)

mechanisms: Acoustic treatment reduces reverberation and overall noise levels, improving perceived comfort and speech intelligibility.
Spatial density influences overall noise generation and perceived crowding, affecting annoyance.
Different learning space layouts (traditional vs. flexible) influence activity patterns, social interaction, and inherent noise levels, shaping acoustic perception and preference.
Quieter internal environments (due to absorption) can make external noise sources more salient and annoying.
Higher background noise levels contribute to a general sense of discomfort and amplify annoyance from specific internal and external noise sources.
moderators: Type of learning space (traditional vs. flexible)
implementation_implications: Architectural design and acoustic conditioning are crucial for optimizing the acoustic experience in educational spaces.
Designers should consider both architectural layout and acoustic treatment to support contemporary pedagogical approaches and student well-being.
Background noise levels should be managed to be below recommended thresholds (e.g., 55 dBA for primary schools).
Acoustic absorption materials are important for improving hearing ability and reducing annoyance from internal noise sources.
Spatial density should be carefully considered to avoid negative impacts on acoustic perception and reduce noise annoyance.

limitations: The small number of learning spaces with acoustic treatment (due to lack of regulatory requirements in Chile and school willingness to participate) limits generalizability of conclusions regarding acoustic treatment impact.
Students (8-11 years old) may have faced post-COVID-19 challenges in reading comprehension, potentially introducing bias in questionnaire responses despite teacher assistance.

Occupant noise levels were measured only during the survey procedure; more accurate conclusions might require noise situation measurements during different lesson scenarios (e.g., teacher presentation, group work).
